prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints and asset prices amplify and propagate shocks into persistent credit cycles

statement.case_for: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) identified a specific, general mechanism: when credit is limited by collateral and collateral values depend on asset prices, a small shock to net worth produces large, persistent and spreading effects on output and investment. The idea is conceptually clean and has been absorbed into the standard way economists model credit frictions. It has shaped the quantitative macro-financial models and policy analysis used since 2008. Nearly three decades of extension and use mean timing is not a concern. Under the criterion I care about most, a contribution that pairs a new explanatory framework with lasting empirical and policy influence, this is the strongest case in the shortlist. Most colleagues' rankings place it at or near the top, but I weigh that only as a prompt to re-check the science, not as evidence of merit. After hearing the attribution arguments I have changed my opening three-name proposal to the two originators.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises, which may make the committee see the macro-finance area as recently honoured. The collateral channel is also hard to identify directly in data. Empirical support is clearer in crisis episodes than in ordinary times, so the mechanism is better established as theory than as a measured magnitude. Finally, the financial-accelerator lineage (Bernanke-Gertler, Gilchrist) is closely related, and any two-name award has to explain why that strand is not credited.

responses.point: Credit Cycles (1997) is a clear two-author contribution. The Gertler-Gilchrist financial-accelerator strand overlaps with what the 2022 prize recognised, so they should not be added here.
responses.response: This persuades me to move from my opening three-name proposal. The originating idea, the feedback loop between collateral values and credit limits, belongs to Kiyotaki and Moore alone. I earlier argued that Gertler's independent contributions justify a third name, and I still think they are real, notably his work on credit frictions in monetary-policy models. But they are mostly extensions and applications of that mechanism, and the accelerator strand is entangled with work the 2022 prize touched. I do not fully share your view that the area is partly covered, though. The 2022 citation concerned banks and the Depression-era analysis of financial crises, not the dynamic amplification of shocks through collateral constraints. So I would treat overlap as a framing issue for the citation, not a reason to downgrade the achievement.

responses.point: The credit-cycles model is general and tractable, and it became a foundation for financial-friction DSGE models. Limiting the award to Kiyotaki and Moore keeps attribution clean.
responses.response: I agree on both the scientific importance and the clean attribution. I would add one qualification to your emphasis on DSGE use. The strongest evidence for the mechanism's importance is its repeated reuse as a modelling building block, not direct identification of the collateral channel in micro data. So the citation should credit the mechanism, not a measured effect size. My own empirical-labour background makes me want the committee to be explicit about this limit, and it is why I list identification as an open uncertainty. It does not change my ranking.

responses.point: The Autor-Hanson-Katz work on tasks and trade shocks rests on transparent, widely stress-tested designs, with Katz as the long-running anchor on skill-biased change and Dorn a more junior co-author.
responses.response: I share your view that B014 is the strongest labour candidate, which is why I keep it as my first alternative. The replication and robustness record you describe is a real strength. Where I would qualify is on maturity and overlap. Persistence and magnitude of the China-shock effects are still debated, and the task framework sits close to work recognised in 2024 and the 2023 labour-history prize. That makes the incremental credit harder to isolate than for Kiyotaki and Moore. On names, I still prefer Katz to Dorn for a three-person group because of his foundational role in the skill-premium literature. Hassler's choice of Dorn over Katz is a defensible judgment call, and the committee would need to settle it explicitly.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises as covering enough adjacent ground to lower the priority of the collateral-constraint mechanism.
Whether leaving out Gertler (and Gilchrist) gives a fair account of the financial-accelerator lineage, given his credit is also split with the New Keynesian entry B019.
How far the collateral channel is identified empirically outside crisis episodes, as opposed to being a widely used theoretical mechanism.

If B011 is not preferred, whether B014 or B026 is the better choice. B014 faces overlap with the 2023 and 2024 prizes and a contested China-shock literature, and B026 has a shorter confirmation record and relies on restricted administrative data.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. None of the credited names for B011, B014 or B026 appear among her listed frequent co-authors. Her field of labour economics and the economics of crime is adjacent to B014 and B026, but that is a field proximity and not a personal connection. It is noted so that her ranking of B014 and B026 is read with that in mind.
